title: The salt doll and the ocean
hookLine: a doll made of salt walks into the sea to measure how deep it is
carry: brahman is known by melting, not measuring
last: THE SNAKE THAT WAS TOLD NOT TO BITE.

lines: IT GOES TO MEASURE THE OCEAN.
cards: A doll made entirely of salt sets out to measure the ocean. Small doll, big job: find out how deep the water goes, then come back and report. It walks down to the shore and steps in.
And right there the story stops being about measuring, because the moment the doll is in the water, it starts to dissolve.
Ramakrishna told this little parable when people asked him a question that sounds simple: what is God like, really?

teach.b: His visitors were often educated men, used to debating. They wanted a definition. He gave them pictures instead, and the Gospel of Sri Ramakrishna, the book of his conversations, is full of them.
The salt doll went to measure the ocean, and it melted.

teach.h: NO ONE COMES BACK TO REPORT.
teach.b: So who was left to come back and say how deep it was? That is his answer about Brahman, the reality the Upanishads point to beyond every name.

You can't stand outside it and take its measurements, because the one measuring is made of the same stuff. Get close enough, and the measurer is gone. He makes the same point another way, and it's startling.
Everything, he says, has become uchchhishta, food that has already been tasted: leftovers. The Vedas, the scriptures, the philosophies have all passed through human mouths.
Only Brahman has never been made leftover, because no one has ever been able to say what it is. Notice what he isn't saying. He isn't throwing scripture away.
He sang hymns, quoted the sacred books, and worshiped the Mother in the temple.
Words point, and what they point to is bigger than any mouth. And the parable isn't a sad one. The doll goes in because it wants to know.
Many readers hear in it the Upanishads' great teaching that atman, your deepest self, and Brahman are not two: a doll of salt came from the sea in the first place. Its not coming back is the answer.

how: Devotees read the Gospel of Sri Ramakrishna in study circles and at centers of the Ramakrishna order, and his parables, like the salt doll, are retold in talks and at home.

o: a sage who wrote a long commentary on the Upanishads
the Dakshineswar priest who taught with small pictures
a Bengali poet who wrote the Gospel down himself

games.q: the salt doll — tap the pairs.
p: the self: salt from the same sea

s: the salt doll came back and reported the ocean's depth
it melted as it went in, so no one was left to report.
Ramakrishna said only Brahman has never been made leftover
because no one has ever been able to say what it is.
the parable means scripture is worthless
he sang hymns and quoted scripture; his point is that words point beyond themselves.

games.q: you're the salt doll, standing at the edge of the sea with a job: measure how deep it goes. what happens?
o: you wade in, measure, and come back.
you step in, and dissolve into the water.
you measure from the shore and guess.
games.why: the doll melts the moment it enters. for Ramakrishna, that's the point: the one who goes to measure Brahman doesn't come back separate.

practice: Bring to mind something you love that you've never managed to explain well: a person, a place, a piece of music, or, if you pray, God. Try silently to describe it in one sentence, and notice how the sentence falls short.
Then let the sentence go, and simply stay near the thing itself, the way the doll stood at the water's edge.

wordCard.voice: Ramakrishna. The temple priest at Dakshineswar who answered hard questions with small pictures. Today's picture: the salt doll that went to measure the ocean.

orig.note: Sanskrit (used in Bengali too): food already tasted, leftovers. Ramakrishna said everything but Brahman has become this.

carryVoice: Your line: Brahman is known by melting, not measuring. Tomorrow, a lizard that won't stay one color. Rest well.
